claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
Changing between oxidizing and reducing gases governs the alloy's degradation mechanism during high-temperature exposure.
An oxidizing atmosphere causes preferential oxidation at grain boundaries.
Ti and Cr are preferentially oxidized at grain boundaries under the proposed oxidizing conditions.
Preferential grain-boundary oxidation produces continuous, brittle oxide films.
Continuous grain-boundary oxide films impair intergranular cohesion and initiate cracks.
Crack initiation at oxidized grain boundaries can lead to rapid catastrophic failure.
A hydrogen-rich reducing atmosphere limits surface oxidation.
Under reducing conditions, diffusion-driven phase coarsening and void nucleation occur internally.
Internal phase coarsening and void formation cause gradual degradation of mechanical integrity.
The as-built alloy has a uniform, fine-grained fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains minimal secondary phases.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more pronounced grain-boundary oxidation than the as-built baseline.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce ductility and fracture toughness and promote brittle failure relative to the as-built baseline.
Reducing exposure will result in minimal surface oxidation but measurable internal coarsening and void formation.
Reducing exposure will cause a gradual decline in mechanical properties relative to the as-built baseline.
The proposed behavior applies at approximately 700 degrees Celsius for exposure durations of 50 to 150 hours.
Oxidation kinetics and diffusion-driven microstructural evolution are significant within the proposed temperature and duration range.
